Fix $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $n\geq0$. A **rank-$n$
$\mathbb F$-vector bundle** over $X$ is a locally trivial bundle
$p:E\to X$ in the sense of [[def-locally-trivial-fiber-bundle]], together with
an $\mathbb F$-vector-space structure on every fiber $E_x=p^{-1}(x)$, whose local charts

$$\phi_i:p^{-1}(U_i)\xrightarrow{\cong}U_i\times\mathbb F^n$$

restrict on every fiber to linear isomorphisms $E_x\cong\mathbb F^n$. Here
$M_n(\mathbb F)\cong\mathbb F^{n^2}$ has its Euclidean topology and
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F)$ has the subspace topology; its underlying
algebraic set is the one fixed in
[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]. The transition
from chart $\phi_i$ to $\phi_j$ is therefore

$$\phi_j\phi_i^{-1}(x,v)=(x,g_{ji}(x)v)$$

for a continuous $g_{ji}:U_i\cap U_j\to\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F)$.
Indeed, evaluating the continuous chart change at each standard basis vector
gives the matrix columns continuously, and its values are invertible because
the chart change is fiberwise linear.
Our index convention gives

$$g_{ii}=I,\qquad g_{ki}=g_{kj}g_{ji}.$$

Rank is fixed in this definition. The case $n=0$ is the bundle $X\to X$
with zero-dimensional fibers, and $X=\varnothing$ is allowed.

The bundle is **numerable** if it has a linear trivializing cover
$(U_i)$ together with a locally finite partition of unity $(\rho_i)$ such
that $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i\subseteq U_i$. The charts and the subordinate
partition, when specified, are called a **numeration**.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $\mathcal U$ be an open cover of $X$. A
family $\{\varphi_s:X\to[0,1]\}_{s\in S}$ is a **partition of unity** when each
$\varphi_s$ is continuous, the family of cozero sets
$\{\operatorname{coz}(\varphi_s)\}_{s\in S}$ is locally finite, and
$$\sum_{s\in S}\varphi_s(x)=1\quad\text{for every }x\in X.$$
The sum is unambiguous because local finiteness says that only finitely many
summands are nonzero near, and hence at, any fixed point.

It is **subordinate to $\mathcal U$** when for every $s\in S$ some
$U\in\mathcal U$ contains the support
$$\operatorname{supp}(\varphi_s):=\overline{\operatorname{coz}(\varphi_s)}.$$
Here cozero sets and zero sets have the meanings of
[[def-zero-sets-and-cozero-sets]].

derivations.claim: If $X=\varnothing$, the conclusion is vacuous; assume $X$ is nonempty. For each $i$ define the $i$th component of $\Phi:E\to X\times\mathbb R^{rs}$ over $x$ by $\sqrt{\rho_i(x)}\tau_i(v)$ when $x\in U_i$, and by zero when $x\notin U_i$. The real square-root function is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ (away from zero, $|\sqrt a-\sqrt b|=|a-b|/(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)$; at zero, $0\le\sqrt a<\varepsilon$ whenever $0\le a<\varepsilon^2$). Because $\operatorname{supp}(\rho_i)\subseteq U_i$, every point outside $U_i$ has a neighborhood on which $\rho_i=0$; hence extending the chart component by zero is continuous there, and within $U_i$ it is a product of continuous coordinate functions. Hence each component, and therefore $\Phi$, is continuous. It is fiberwise linear.

If $v\in E_x$ is nonzero, the partition identity gives some $i$ with $\rho_i(x)>0$. Then $x\in U_i$ and [F1] makes $\tau_i(v)\ne0$, so the $i$th component of $\Phi_x(v)$ is nonzero. Thus each $\Phi_x$ is injective and has rank $r$.

In local bundle coordinates, the matrix of $\Phi$ has rank $r$ at every point. At any chosen $x$, some $r\times r$ minor is nonzero; continuity keeps that minor nonzero on a neighborhood. After reordering the target coordinates, the image there is the graph of a continuous matrix over $\mathbb R^r$. Thus $E'=\Phi(E)$ is a rank-$r$ subbundle of the trivial bundle.

On a neighborhood with a continuous frame matrix $Q$ for $E'$, the orthogonal projection onto $E'$ is $P=Q(Q^{\mathsf T}Q)^{-1}Q^{\mathsf T}$. The Gram matrix $Q^{\mathsf T}Q$ is positive definite and invertible; its inverse varies continuously because each inverse entry is a cofactor divided by the nonzero determinant, so $P$ is continuous. Therefore $I-P$ has locally constant rank $rs-r$ and its image is a subbundle $F=E'^{\perp}$. Fiberwise orthogonal decomposition gives $E'\oplus F=X\times\mathbb R^{rs}$, and $\Phi$ identifies $E$ with $E'$. If $r=0$, take $E'=0$ and $F=X\times\mathbb R^0$.

A **CW complex** is a Hausdorff space $X$ with a filtration
$$\varnothing=X^{-1}\subseteq X^0\subseteq X^1\subseteq\cdots,\qquad X=\bigcup_{n\geq0}X^n,$$
where $X^0$ is discrete and $X^n$ is obtained from $X^{n-1}$ by attaching a (possibly infinite) family of $n$-disks along maps $S^{n-1}\to X^{n-1}$ as in [[def-cell-attachment-by-a-characteristic-map]]. The images of the disk interiors are its **open $n$-cells** $e^n_\alpha$, and the disk maps are their characteristic maps. It moreover satisfies: (C) each closed cell $\overline {e^n_\alpha}$ meets only finitely many cells; and (W) $A\subseteq X$ is closed exactly when $A\cap\overline e$ is closed in $\overline e$ for every cell $e$. These are closure finiteness and the weak topology.
Every compact topological space is paracompact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Dependent Choice. Every open cover
of a paracompact Hausdorff space admits a locally finite partition of unity
subordinate to it.

In ZF, the Axiom of Choice implies the prescribed-initial-point form of the
Axiom of Dependent Choice. Explicitly, if $X$ is nonempty, $R$ is an entire
relation on $X$, and $a\in X$, then AC supplies a sequence
$x:\mathbb N\to X$ such that

$$x_0=a\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_n\mathbin R x_{n+1}$$

for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Consequently, a vector-bundle theorem stated under
AC may discharge a separately declared DC hypothesis without assuming another
choice principle.

Let $X$ be compact Hausdorff and let $E\to X$ be a rank-$r$ real vector bundle with a finite linear trivializing cover $(U_i,\tau_i)$ and a subordinate finite partition of unity $(\rho_i)$. Then some $N$ and a bundle $F\to X$ satisfy $E\oplus F\cong X\times\mathbb R^N$. The embedding and orthogonal complement construction uses only the supplied finite numeration.

derivations.claim: If $X$ is empty, the claim is vacuous; assume it is nonempty. Each closed cell of $X$ is the continuous image of a closed disk and hence compact. Since there are finitely many cells, $X$ is a finite union of compact closed-cell images, so it is compact; [F1] gives Hausdorffness.

By [F2] and step 1.1, $X$ is paracompact and Hausdorff. The bundle's local trivializations form an open cover of $X$. Compactness gives a finite subcover. Apply [F3] to this cover: its AC and DC hypotheses hold because AC is given and [F4] derives DC. The resulting locally finite partition has only finitely many nonzero members: choose for each point a neighborhood meeting finitely many supports, then take a finite subcover of those neighborhoods by compactness; the union of the finite index sets is finite. Thus the chart subcover and partition give a finite numeration.

Apply [F5] to this finite numeration. It supplies a fiberwise-linear embedding $E\hookrightarrow X\times\mathbb R^N$ and the subbundle $F$ orthogonal to its image in the standard Euclidean metric. The fiberwise orthogonal direct sum is the whole trivial bundle, so $E\oplus F\cong X\times\mathbb R^N$. AC is used to obtain the partition in [F3] and, through [F4], to discharge its DC hypothesis in step 2.1.

**Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice** ([[def-dependent-choice]]). Let
$(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space.

1. If $X$ is normal ([[def-normal-and-t4-spaces]]), $A \subseteq X$ is closed
   ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and $a \le b$ are reals, then every
   continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) extends to a continuous
   $F : X \to [a,b]$ with $F|_A = f$.
2. Conversely, if for every closed $A \subseteq X$ and every reals $a \le b$
   every continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$ extends to a continuous $F : X \to [a,b]$
   with $F|_A = f$, then $X$ is normal. **This direction uses no choice
   principle.**

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Finite CW spaces are compact Hausdorff and hence normal. For completeness, disjoint closed subsets in a compact Hausdorff space have disjoint open neighborhoods: separate a fixed point of the first set from every point of the second, take a finite subcover of the second and intersect the corresponding first neighborhoods, then take a finite subcover of the first and intersect the corresponding second neighborhoods. For a general compact Hausdorff base, a finite trivializing cover and [F4] give a finite numeration: a locally finite family on a compact space has only finitely many nonempty supports. The real weighted chart embedding $v\mapsto(\sqrt{\rho_i(x)}\tau_i(v))_i$ is continuous by support subordination and injective because a partition member is positive. In local coordinates its full-rank matrix $Q$ has continuous projection $Q(Q^{\mathsf T}Q)^{-1}Q^{\mathsf T}$, whose orthogonal complement is a bundle. Thus [F1]'s complement statement extends to compact Hausdorff bases. Apply this on each of the finitely many clopen rank strata, enlarging their trivial ambient ranks to a common integer. Group completion says $[E]=[F]$ iff $E\oplus G\cong F\oplus G$ for some $G$. Adding a complement of $G$ turns this into $E\oplus\varepsilon^k\cong F\oplus\varepsilon^k$; the converse is immediate in the group.

We record the extension argument used below. Embed $E$ into $X\times\mathbb R^N$ with projection $P(x)$, and suppose a frame $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ is supplied on a closed subset $B$ on which $E$ has rank $n$. Its finitely many ambient coordinate functions are bounded, so [F3] extends them to vectors $\widehat s_i$ on $X$. The sections $P\widehat s_i$ extend the frame. Their Gram determinant is nonzero on $B$, and thus on an open neighborhood $U$ of $B$ lying in the rank-$n$ stratum. They form a frame on $U$. This also extends a prescribed bundle homomorphism: embed its target in a trivial bundle, extend the matrix entries from $B$, and project to the target. For a map between nontrivial source bundles apply the same argument to its Hom bundle, which is a finite-rank real bundle. Apply the construction on $X\times I$ for families. AC is used through [F1] and the implication AC to DC in [F3].

Add the elementary triple $(F',F',1)$ where $F\oplus F'\cong\varepsilon^n$. Every triple is thereby represented by $(H,\varepsilon^n,\tau)$ with $\tau:H|_A\cong A\times\mathbb R^n$. Extend this trivialization over a neighborhood $U$ by step 2.1. Collapse the fibers of $H$ above $A$ using $\tau$ to one copy of $\mathbb R^n$. This gives a bundle $\bar H$ on $X/A$: on $q(U)$ use the extended frame, and elsewhere use the old charts. Here $q(U)$ is open because $U$ contains $A$ and is saturated. The transition maps near the collapsed point are continuous by the quotient topology. Define the triple class to be $[\bar H]-[\varepsilon^n]$. Its fiber difference at the basepoint is zero. If $A$ is empty this means $[H]-[\varepsilon^n]$ on $X$, extended by zero to the extra point.

The collapse construction is intrinsic to the relation $(a,v)\sim(a',v')$ iff $\tau(v)=\tau(v')$; hence its bundle isomorphism class does not depend on the neighborhood or extension frame. We spell out invariance under a global gauge, since it need not be constant on $A$. Suppose the normalized frame changes from $\tau$ to $b|_A\tau$, where $b:X\to GL_n(\mathbb R)$. Add a trivial $n$-plane to $H$. On a framed neighborhood $U$ of $A$, the two-block rotation contracts $\operatorname{diag}(b^{-1},b)$ to identity: use $\operatorname{diag}(b^{-1},I)R_t\operatorname{diag}(I,b)R_t^{-1}$. Choose a continuous cutoff equal to one on $A$ with support in $U$, which exists by first shrinking to $A\subset W\subset\overline W\subset U$ using normality and then extending the values one on $A$ and zero on $X\setminus W$ by [F3], and use it to run this contraction backwards only near $A$. This defines a global automorphism $c$ of $H\oplus\varepsilon^n$ restricting in its old frame to $\operatorname{diag}(b^{-1},b)$ on $A$. Multiply $c$ on the left by the global automorphism that is identity on $H$ and $b^{-1}$ on the added trivial factor. The resulting automorphism restricts to $\operatorname{diag}(b^{-1},I)$, so it identifies the two descended stabilized bundles in their collapse frames. Thus they have the same quotient class. Any change of the global trivialization of $F\oplus F'$ is precisely such a gauge. A homotopy of $\tau$ gives the same construction over $(X/A)\times I$; [F2] identifies its endpoint classes. Adding an elementary triple $(G,G,h)$ does not change the result: extend $h$ globally, add a complement of $G$, and use the resulting global frame identification on both entries. The added descended difference is $[\varepsilon^k]-[\varepsilon^k]=0$. Two choices of complement are compared by adding both complements and the same bundle $F$; after the evident permutations each resulting stabilization contains the same globally trivialized summand. Thus the construction respects exactly the listed relations.

Conversely, any reduced class on $Y=X/A$ is $[P]-[Q]$. Complement $Q$ to a trivial bundle, so the class is $[H]-[\varepsilon^n]$. Its reduced condition implies $\operatorname{rank}H_*=n$. Choose a linear identification $H_*\cong\mathbb R^n$. Pullback along $q$ gives $(q^*H,\varepsilon^n,\tau)$, with $\tau$ the constant fiber identification on $A$. Its collapse recovers the original bundle and class. For injectivity suppose two normalized triples collapse to the same class. Their denominators may first be equalized by adding trivial elementary triples. Step 1.1 on the compact Hausdorff quotient $Y$ then gives an isomorphism $\phi:\bar H\oplus\varepsilon^k\to\bar H'\oplus\varepsilon^k$. In the chosen frames its value at $*$ is one matrix $B\in GL_{n+k}(\mathbb R)$. Pull back $\phi$ on the first entries and use the constant automorphism $B$ on the trivial second entries; these form an isomorphism of the stabilized triples. This proves both inverses and injectivity, including rank variations on components disjoint from $A$.

The triple presentation is a group, even if described initially by stable sums: the inverse of $(E,F,g)$ is $(F,E,g^{-1})$. After normalizing $g$ to an isometry, identify the second direct sum with $E\oplus F$ by permutation. The rotation matrix on $E|_A\oplus F|_A$ with diagonal $\cos t$ and off-diagonal $-\sin t\,g^{-1}$ and $\sin t\,g$ connects identity to the off-diagonal interchange. This makes the summed triple elementary up to homotopy. Polar normalization is valid since $g^*g$ is positive definite, and the positive square root varies continuously; one can see the latter locally by the uniformly convergent binomial series after scaling positive matrices to have spectrum in a compact subinterval of $(0,2)$. All collapse operations commute with pullback. A homotopy of pair maps descends to a based homotopy of quotients; [F2] proves the claimed homotopy invariance.

Here are the quaternionic details, rather than an appeal to a complex-only result. By [F4], choose finitely many right-linear charts and a real subordinate partition $\rho_i$, the map $v\mapsto(\sqrt{\rho_i(x)}\,\tau_i(v))_i$ embeds a right-$\mathbb H$ bundle in a finite trivial right-$\mathbb H$ bundle. It is continuous by support subordination and injective because some $\rho_i(x)>0$. In a local full-rank frame $Q$ its orthogonal projection is $Q(Q^*Q)^{-1}Q^*$; this is right-linear, and continuous because the inverse, viewed in real coordinates, is continuous by the cofactor formula. Orthogonal complements are therefore right-$\mathbb H$ subbundles. For homotopy invariance on compact $X\times I$, use this embedding and its projection $P(x,t)$. Compactness gives a subdivision for which $\|P(x,t_{i+1})-P(x,t_i)\|<1$ uniformly in $x$. Projection between the two image bundles is injective by this inequality and hence an isomorphism; these right-linear isomorphisms compose to identify endpoints. For extending a Hom section in step 2.1, embed the Hom bundle as a real bundle and extend its real coordinates; it is the bundle of right-linear maps, so the resulting section is right-linear. All the collapse, stabilization and rotation arguments above now apply over $\mathbb H$. This proves the quaternionic statements independently.

Relations are bundle isomorphism, direct-sum additivity, homotopy of $g$, and deletion of a triple whose $g$ extends to an isomorphism on $X$. Equivalently, use stable homotopy of triples, allowing addition of such elementary triples. Pullback along homotopic maps of pairs induces equal maps. In degree zero over $X$, equality of virtual bundles is equality after common trivial stabilization. Every real bundle on $X$ has a finite trivial complement. The analogous complement, stable-isomorphism, homotopy and triple statements hold for right-$\mathbb H$ bundles. All these conclusions also hold for compact Hausdorff pairs with closed subspace; this includes disk, sphere and Thom bundle spaces over compact finite CW bases.

If $(X,A)$ is a relative CW complex, then $A\hookrightarrow X$ has the homotopy extension property; in particular it is a cofibration.

Explicitly, for every topological space $Y$, continuous $g:X\to Y$, and continuous $H:A\times I\to Y$ satisfying $H(a,0)=g(a)$, there is a continuous $\widetilde H:X\times I\to Y$ restricting to $H$ on $A\times I$ and to $g$ at time zero. Here $I=[0,1]$ and products have their ordinary product topologies. There is no finiteness or dimension bound on the CW complex, no separation hypothesis on $Y$, and no choice assumption. The CW structure, including its characteristic maps, is supplied as data.
For a based cofibration $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ in CGWH, the canonical map $\psi:C_i\to X/A$, collapsing the cone CA, is a based homotopy equivalence.

For a based map $f:X\to Y$ of well-pointed CGWH spaces, put $i:Y\to C_f$ and let $j:C_f\to C_i$ be the next cofiber inclusion. The collapse $\psi:C_i\to\Sigma X$ is a based homotopy equivalence with $\psi\circ j=q$, where $q:C_f\to\Sigma X$ collapses $Y$. Under it, the next cofiber map agrees up to based homotopy with $-\Sigma f$. Suspension commutes with cone formation, with the two-coordinate interchange in the quotient map retained.

For a well-pointed CGWH based space $(X,x_0)$ set
$$CX=(X\times I)/(X\times\{1\}\cup\{x_0\}\times I),\qquad \Sigma X=CX/(X\times\{0\}).$$
The common collapsed set is the basepoint; the copy of X at height zero is the cone base. All products and mapping conventions are those of [[def-compactly-generated-conventions-for-based-homotopy]], and well-pointedness means [[def-cofibration-and-homotopy-extension-property]].

Write $\rho_X([x,t])=[x,1-t]$ and $-\Sigma f=\rho_Y\Sigma f$. The cofiber sequence convention is
$$X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{i}C_f\xrightarrow{q}\Sigma X\xrightarrow{-\Sigma f}\Sigma Y\xrightarrow{-\Sigma i}\Sigma C_f\xrightarrow{-\Sigma q}\Sigma^2X\xrightarrow{\Sigma^2 f}\Sigma^2Y\longrightarrow\cdots.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be $\mathrm{SO}(p)$ or a Clifford centriole with normalized trace metric and indicated antipodal pole pair in one component. In a fixed endpoint-path component suppose every geodesic which is not energy-minimizing in that component has index at least $d+1$. Then the inclusion of constant-speed minimizing geodesics into the $H^1$ path space, and into the continuous compact-open path space, is $d$-connected: every map of a finite CW pair $(K,A)$ with $\dim K\le d$, taking $A$ to the minima, deforms relative to $A$ into the minima.

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be a nonminimizing endpoint-fixed geodesic from $J_l$ to $-J_l$ in a Clifford centriole $P_l$, with the normalized trace metric. Let $s_j$ be the real dimension of an irreducible negative-square Clifford module. If $l\not\equiv2\pmod4$, then $\operatorname{ind}\gamma\ge p/s_{l+1}-1$. If $l=4m-2$, let $w$ be determinant winding under $J\mapsto JJ_l^{-1}$ into $\mathrm U(p/2)$. For $d>0$, the inequality $p-4|w|\ge4d s_l$ implies $\operatorname{ind}\gamma>d$. The first estimate is non-strict; its use for connectivity requires additional strict slack.

If $(X,A)$ is a relative CW complex, then $A\hookrightarrow X$ has the homotopy extension property; in particular it is a cofibration.

Explicitly, for every topological space $Y$, continuous $g:X\to Y$, and continuous $H:A\times I\to Y$ satisfying $H(a,0)=g(a)$, there is a continuous $\widetilde H:X\times I\to Y$ restricting to $H$ on $A\times I$ and to $g$ at time zero. Here $I=[0,1]$ and products have their ordinary product topologies. There is no finiteness or dimension bound on the CW complex, no separation hypothesis on $Y$, and no choice assumption. The CW structure, including its characteristic maps, is supplied as data.

Assume AC and let $p\ge2$ be even. Let $V\to X$ be a finite-rank Euclidean real vector bundle and put $C(V)=\mathrm{Cl}(V,-\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$, so each vector $v$ acts with square $-\lVert v\rVert^2$. An **ungraded** $C(V)$-module bundle is a finite-rank real vector bundle with continuous fiberwise unital Clifford action. Write $K_{C(V)}(X)$ for the Grothendieck group of their direct-sum monoid.

A **graded** $C(V)$-module bundle is a module $\Lambda=\Lambda^0\oplus\Lambda^1$ whose action satisfies $C(V)^i\Lambda^j\subseteq\Lambda^{i+j}$, with indices modulo two. In particular vector multiplication is odd: it exchanges the two parity subbundles. Write $M(V)$ for the Grothendieck group of graded modules. The same convention gives $M_n$ for the negative Clifford algebra $C_n=\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n}$ over a point. Ungraded $K_{C(V)}(X)$ and graded $M(V)$ are distinct groups; neither is identified with the other by notation. The rank-$4m$ volume Thom theorem uses the former, whereas ABS uses a restriction quotient of the latter.

Let $k,V,B,Q$ be as in [[def-clifford-algebra-of-a-quadratic-space]], and let $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. Then

$$\bar v\bar w+\bar w\bar v=2B(v,w)1$$

for all $v,w\in V$.

Let $\xi=(E\xrightarrow\pi B,h)$ be a rank-$n$ real vector bundle equipped
with a continuous fiber metric.  Define
$$D_h(\xi)=\{v\in E:\|v\|_h\leq1\},\quad S_h(\xi)=\{v\in E:\|v\|_h=1\},$$
and define the Thom space by the based quotient
$$\operatorname{Th}_h(\xi)=D_h(\xi)/S_h(\xi).$$
Here $X/\varnothing$ means $X_+$, so the rank-zero convention is already
included.

For two supplied metrics $h$ and $k$, the canonical radial homeomorphism of
pairs is
$$r_{h,k}(0_b)=0_b,$$
$$r_{h,k}(v)=\frac{\|v\|_h}{\|v\|_k}v\quad(v\ne0).$$
It preserves the base and normalized radius, has inverse $r_{k,h}$, and
descends to the quotient.  Continuity at the zero section follows in a bundle
chart because the ratio of the two norms on the unit sphere is locally
bounded above and below.  The positive-definite interpolation
$h_t=(1-t)h+tk$ gives the canonical radial isotopy $r_{h,h_t}$.

This definition is choice-free once the metric is supplied.  For the empty
base all three spaces are empty except for the quotient basepoint; for rank
zero, $D_h(\xi)=B$, $S_h(\xi)=\varnothing$, and
$\operatorname{Th}_h(\xi)=B_+$.  The zero vector is fixed, sphere and disk
endpoints are preserved, and the formulas for $h=k$ are the identity.

Let $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $X$, and let
$g_{ji}:U_i\cap U_j\to\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F)$ be continuous maps
such that

$$g_{ii}=I,\qquad g_{ki}=g_{kj}g_{ji}.$$

The quotient of $\coprod_iU_i\times\mathbb F^n$ by
$(x,v,i)\sim(x,g_{ji}(x)v,j)$ is a rank-$n$ $\mathbb F$-vector bundle.
Replacing $g_{ji}$ by $g'_{ji}=h_jg_{ji}h_i^{-1}$ for continuous
$h_i:U_i\to\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F)$ gives an isomorphic bundle.
Every rank-$n$ bundle is recovered from the cocycle of any linear atlas.

Reversing the product order takes $n(n-1)/2=2m(4m-1)$ swaps, an even number; multiplying the $n$ generator squares contributes $(-1)^{4m}=1$. Thus $\omega^2=1$. For any orthonormal frame, pairwise anticommutation makes the product equal to the alternating product $\operatorname{Alt}(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)c(v_{\sigma(1)})\cdots c(v_{\sigma(n)})$. This is an alternating multilinear function of the frame vectors. An oriented orthogonal change has determinant $+1$, so it leaves this top alternating product unchanged. Hence $\omega$ is frame-independent and, in local frames, varies continuously.

Moving any unit vector $v$ past the other $n-1$ orthogonal generators gives $\omega c(v)=(-1)^{n-1}c(v)\omega=-c(v)\omega$. If the module also has a parity grading, $\omega$ has even parity because $n$ is even, so it preserves $\Lambda^0$ and $\Lambda^1$. The continuous maps $p_\pm=(I\pm\omega)/2$ are idempotents with $p_+p_-=0$ and $p_++p_-=I$. In any local frame their matrix entries vary continuously, and the trace of an idempotent equals its rank, so each image rank is locally constant. At a point choose a basis of the image; applying $p_\pm$ to the same frame vectors remains independent on a neighborhood and spans the image there. Thus their images are complementary subbundles (graded when a parity grading is supplied). The anticommutation identity makes $c(v)$ interchange their images, and $c(v)^{-1}=-c(v)$ for $\lVert v\rVert=1$, so the interchange is an isomorphism.

Pull the two eigenbundles back to the two closed disk halves of $S(\mathbb R\oplus V)$. Thicken the halves slightly so their overlap is an equatorial collar; radial projection in each fiber identifies that collar continuously with $S(V)$, so extend the transition $c(v)$ constantly along the radial coordinate. The opposite transition is $-c(v)$, its inverse, and the two-chart cocycle is therefore satisfied. The quotient gluing theorem [F4] gives a vector bundle, and its relative disk/sphere triple is exactly $(\Lambda^+,c(v),\Lambda^-)$. The volume eigenspaces are defined by $\omega$, whereas an additional parity grading is the grading operator in [F1]; these are distinct constructions, and no identification between them is assumed.

For a quaternionic bundle $E$ the same calculation is valid in the balanced tensor product since $\omega$ and $c(v)$ commute with the right scalar action on $\Sigma$. Let $V\to X$ be a finite-rank Euclidean real vector bundle and put $C(V)=\mathrm{Cl}(V,-\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$, so each vector $v$ acts with square $-\lVert v\rVert^2$. An **ungraded** $C(V)$-module bundle is a finite-rank real vector bundle with continuous fiberwise unital Clifford action. Write $K_{C(V)}(X)$ for the Grothendieck group of their direct-sum monoid.

A **graded** $C(V)$-module bundle is a module $\Lambda=\Lambda^0\oplus\Lambda^1$ whose action satisfies $C(V)^i\Lambda^j\subseteq\Lambda^{i+j}$, with indices modulo two. In particular vector multiplication is odd: it exchanges the two parity subbundles. Write $M(V)$ for the Grothendieck group of graded modules. The same convention gives $M_n$ for the negative Clifford algebra $C_n=\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n}$ over a point. Ungraded $K_{C(V)}(X)$ and graded $M(V)$ are distinct groups; neither is identified with the other by notation. The rank-$4m$ volume Thom theorem uses the former, whereas ABS uses a restriction quotient of the latter.

Use the plus-square convention $v^2=Q(v)1$. For the real standard form $Q_{p,q}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p x_i^2-\sum_{j=1}^q x_{p+j}^2$, write $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0$ for the even part of the canonical $\mathbb Z/2$ grading. If $p>0$, then

$$
\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0\cong \mathrm{Cl}_{q,p-1};
$$

if $p=0$ and $q>0$, then $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q}^0\cong\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q-1}$. For the standard complex form $Q_n(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2$ with $n>0$, the even subalgebra is isomorphic over $\mathbb C$ to $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n-1}(\mathbb C)$, the complex Clifford algebra on $n-1$ generators each having square $-1$, and hence to the standard complex Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}_{n-1}(\mathbb C)$.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic not $2$, let $V$ be finite-dimensional of dimension $n$, and let $B$ be any symmetric bilinear form on $V$, possibly degenerate; put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Fix an ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$. Then

$$1,\qquad \bar e_{i_1}\cdots\bar e_{i_r}\quad(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n)$$

is a $k$-basis of $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$, so $\dim_k\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=2^n$. Give $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ the word-length filtration $F_{-1}=0$ and, for $m\ge0$, let $F_m$ be the span of products of at most $m$ canonical generators. The natural graded algebra map

$$\Lambda V\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}_F\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}F_m/F_{m-1}$$

that sends $v\in V$ to the degree-one class of $\bar v$ is an isomorphism, where the graded product is induced by $F_pF_q\subseteq F_{p+q}$. No nondegeneracy hypothesis is needed.

For n≥0 put C_n=Cl(ℝ^n,−‖·‖²). Let M_n be the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional real Z/2-graded left C_n-modules and let r_n:M_{n+1}→M_n be restriction along the standard inclusion of the first n Clifford generators. Define A_n=coker(r_n). For n=0 the grading is retained, so M_0≅Z⊕Z from even and odd dimensions; no parity type is identified with a volume-element eigenspace.

derivations.claim: Let $e_n$ be the last standard generator. It is odd and invertible because $e_n^2=-1$. Multiplication by $e_n$ maps $C_n^0$ bijectively onto $C_n^1$, with inverse multiplication by $-e_n$; thus $C_n^1=e_nC_n^0$. By [F2], the action of $C_n^0$ on $M^0$ makes it an ungraded $C_{n-1}$-module.

Define $G(N)=C_n\otimes_{C_n^0}N$, with parity inherited from $C_n$ and the $C_{n-1}$-action transported along the algebra isomorphism in [F2]. Because $C_n=C_n^0\oplus e_nC_n^0$ as a right $C_n^0$-module, its even part is canonically $N$ and its odd part is $e_n\otimes N$. Hence $G(N)$ is finite-dimensional and taking its even part returns $N$.

For $M$, define evaluation $\varepsilon:C_n\otimes_{C_n^0}M^0\to M$ by $a\otimes m\mapsto am$. It is well-defined because $ab\otimes m=a\otimes bm$ for $b\in C_n^0$. On the even part it is the canonical isomorphism $C_n^0\otimes_{C_n^0}M^0\cong M^0$. On the odd part it sends $e_n\otimes m$ to $e_nm$; this is bijective since $e_n:M^0\to M^1$ has inverse $-e_n$. Therefore evaluation is an even graded $C_n$-module isomorphism.

The restriction functor $M\mapsto M^0$ and induction $N\mapsto C_n\otimes_{C_n^0}N$ are inverse up to the natural isomorphisms in steps 2.1 and 2.2, so they give an equivalence. At $n=0$, $C_0=\mathbb R$ is purely even; a one-dimensional module concentrated in odd parity has even part zero, while a one-dimensional even module has even part $\mathbb R$. Thus the same equivalence fails at $n=0$, and the two parity generators must remain distinct in $M_0\cong\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z$.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

subinterval gives the full jump form

present in the integrated form; it cancels with the corresponding jump created
when that form is integrated back to the derivative-product expression. If
the endpoints are fixed for every $(s,r)$, then $D_sW(a)=D_sW(b)=0$, so the

Composing it with the stabilized $\phi$ gives upper gauge $U^{-1}U=I$, as required.

Let $n=p+q$, let $r$ be the residue of $p-q$ modulo $8$ in $\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$, and use $v^2=Q(v)1$ with signature ordered $(+^p,-^q)$. For every nondegenerate real form of signature $(p,q)$, the real Clifford algebra is

| $r$ | parity of $n$ | $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}$ |
|---:|:---:|---|
| $0$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $1$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $2$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $3$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |
| $4$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $5$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)\oplus M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $6$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $7$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |

Only signatures with $p,q\ge0$ are considered; in the feasible rows the displayed exponents are nonnegative. For a nondegenerate complex quadratic form on dimension $n$, its Clifford algebra is

$$\mathrm{Cl}_n(\mathbb C)\cong\begin{cases}M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ even},\\M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}$$

These matrix-algebra classifications require nondegeneracy; no such classification is asserted for degenerate forms.

A finite-dimensional free-fermion Hamiltonian is a self-adjoint matrix on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. It is gapped at zero if 0 is not in its spectrum. A symmetry class is specified by named unitary and antiunitary operators and exact commutation, anticommutation and square relations with H. Stable equivalence means gap-preserving homotopy after direct sum with fixed reference trivial bands; phases are differences of stabilized systems, not absolute modules.

Class A has no additional antiunitary constraint. A symmetry is unitary or antiunitary and its relation is recorded as S H S^{-1}=σH, σ∈{+1,−1}; any additional square relation is part of the declared model data.

Assume AC. For a finite CW pair $(X,A)$, $KO^0(X,A)$ is naturally the group of triples $(E,F,g)$, with $E,F$ real bundles on $X$ and $g:E|_A\to F|_A$ an isomorphism. Relations are bundle isomorphism, direct-sum additivity, homotopy of $g$, and deletion of a triple whose $g$ extends to an isomorphism on $X$. Equivalently, use stable homotopy of triples, allowing addition of such elementary triples. Pullback along homotopic maps of pairs induces equal maps. In degree zero over $X$, equality of virtual bundles is equality after common trivial stabilization. Every real bundle on $X$ has a finite trivial complement. The analogous complement, stable-isomorphism, homotopy and triple statements hold for right-$\mathbb H$ bundles. All these conclusions also hold for compact Hausdorff pairs with closed subspace; this includes disk, sphere and Thom bundle spaces over compact finite CW bases.

Assume AC. Finite CW pairs have the natural cofiber exact sequence

$$\cdots\longrightarrow KO^{-j-1}(X)\longrightarrow KO^{-j-1}(A)\xrightarrow{\partial}KO^{-j}(X,A)\longrightarrow KO^{-j}(X)\longrightarrow KO^{-j}(A)\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow KO^0(A).$$

This sequence continues indefinitely to the left; a positive-degree continuation requires a separately proved periodicity theorem. The reduced suspension identity is $\widetilde {KO}^{-j}(\Sigma Y)=\widetilde {KO}^{-j-1}(Y)$. There are natural associative products

$$KO^{-p}(X,A)\otimes KO^{-q}(Y,B)\longrightarrow KO^{-p-q}(X\times Y,A\times Y\cup X\times B),$$

which in absolute degree zero are the bundle tensor product. They commute with the suspension identifications with the order of sphere coordinates retained, and interchange of degrees $-p,-q$ has sign $(-1)^{pq}$. The diagonal gives internal products; a real factor acts on relative $KSp$. For a metric bundle $V$, the quotient $\widehat V/s_+(X)$, where $\widehat V=S(\mathbb R\oplus V)$, is naturally homeomorphic to $\operatorname{Th}(V)$. At rank zero both are $X_+$. The reduced groups split $KO^0(Y)=\widetilde {KO}^0(Y)\oplus\mathbb Z$ at a chosen basepoint. The analogous exactness and suspension statements hold for $KSp$.

For a based compact Hausdorff space $(Y,*)$, set $\widetilde {KO}^0(Y)=\ker(KO^0(Y)\to KO^0(*))$. For a compact pair with closed subspace $A\subset X$, set $KO^0(X,A)=\widetilde {KO}^0(X/A)$, where all of $A$ is collapsed to one basepoint. If $A=\varnothing$, use $X_+=X\amalg\{*\}$ instead. Set $KO^{-j}(X,A)=\widetilde {KO}^0(S^j\wedge(X/A))$ for $j\geq0$, and $KO^{-j}(X)=KO^{-j}(X,\varnothing)$. The same conventions define reduced, relative and negative-degree $KSp$.

For a finite-rank metric real bundle $V\to X$ over compact $X$, write $\operatorname{Th}(V)=D(V)/S(V)$ and $KO_c^{-j}(V)=\widetilde {KO}^0(S^j\wedge\operatorname{Th}(V))$. At rank zero use $\operatorname{Th}(0)=X_+$. These definitions do not assert any periodicity or an isomorphism between successive degrees.

Assume AC. Clutching and stabilization give natural additive identifications, for $n\geq1$,

$$\widetilde {KO}^0(S^n)\cong\underset r{\operatorname{colim}}\,\pi_{n-1}(O(r)),\qquad\widetilde {KSp}^0(S^n)\cong\underset r{\operatorname{colim}}\,\pi_{n-1}(Sp(r)).$$

At $n=1$ the right sides mean component groups under block sum. Then $KO^0(*)=KSp^0(*)=\mathbb Z$ by real and quaternionic dimension, respectively, and

$$KO^{-1}(*)=\mathbb Z/2,\qquad KO^{-2}(*)=\mathbb Z/2,\qquad KO^{-3}(*)=0,$$

$$KSp^{-1}(*)=KSp^{-2}(*)=KSp^{-3}(*)=0.$$

Here $Sp(r)$ is the compact group of right-$\mathbb H$-linear isometries of $\mathbb H^r$. These calculations use no Bott periodicity or KO coefficient table.

Let $\mathbb H$ be the quaternions with conjugate $x\mapsto\bar x$ and norm $N$,
let $S^3=\{q\in\mathbb H:N(q)=1\}$ be the unit sphere, and let
$\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H=\mathbb Ri\oplus\mathbb Rj\oplus\mathbb Rk$ carry the
restricted Euclidean inner product, identified with $\mathbb R^3$ through the
basis $(i,j,k)$. Let $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ be the group of real $3\times3$
matrices $R$ with $R^{\mathsf T}R=I$ and $\det R=1$, carrying the subspace
topology of the nine entries, and for $q\in S^3$ let $\rho(q)$ be the linear map
of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ defined by
$$\rho(q)(v)=qvq^{-1},$$
written in the basis $(i,j,k)$ as a real $3\times3$ matrix. Then:

1. $\rho:S^3\to\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is a continuous surjective group
   homomorphism with kernel $\{\pm1\}$, and it is a two-sheeted covering map;
   consequently $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is homeomorphic to the orbit space
   $S^3/\{\pm1\}$.
2. For every covering $p:E\to B$, every $e_0\in E$ and every integer $n\ge2$,
   the induced homomorphism $p_*:\pi_n(E,e_0)\to\pi_n(B,p(e_0))$ is an
   isomorphism. In particular
   $\rho_*:\pi_3(S^3,1)\to\pi_3(\operatorname{SO}(3),I)$ is an isomorphism.
3. $\pi_3(S^3,1)\cong\mathbb Z$ by degree, and $\rho_*$ carries the degree-one
   generator of $\pi_3(S^3,1)$ to the class $[\rho]$; hence
   $\pi_3(\operatorname{SO}(3),I)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\rho]$.
4. The clutching construction over the equatorial $S^3$ with clutching map
   $\rho$ produces an oriented rank-three real vector bundle
   $E_\rho\to S^4$ which is not trivial.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, let $\alpha:I\to B$ be a path, and let $e_0\in E$ satisfy $p(e_0)=\alpha(0)$. There is a unique path $\widetilde\alpha:I\to E$ with $\widetilde\alpha(0)=e_0$ and $p\circ\widetilde\alpha=\alpha$.
Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, $H:Y\times I\to B$ a homotopy, and $\widetilde H_0:Y\to E$ a lift of $H(-,0)$. There is a unique lift $\widetilde H:Y\times I\to E$ of $H$ extending $\widetilde H_0$.

Assume AC. For $M=M^0\oplus M^1$ a graded real $C_n=\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n}$
module, let $a_M(v)=c(v)|_{M^0}:M^0\to M^1$. Its disk/sphere triple
$(\pi^*M^0,\pi^*M^1,a_M)$ gives $s_n(M)\in\widetilde{KO}^0(S^n)$.
For $n=0$ this means the even-minus-odd virtual vector space on $S^0$.
Then

$$\ker s_n=\operatorname{im}(r_n),\qquad \alpha_n:A_n\xrightarrow{\cong}KO^{-n}(\mathrm{pt}).$$

The maps are multiplicative under the graded tensor product. The chosen
degree-eight algebraic generator maps to the same $\beta$ that supplies

is a premise.

Assume AC. The real branch is compatible with direct sums and products of spinor

derivations.claim: Transport $H_0$ by $w$ so that both masses act on the same fixed representation. Define first an auxiliary comparison $\Phi_q$ with the positive-rank convention, and finally set $\Psi_q=-\Phi_q$ in EVERY degree. For $q=0$ put $\Phi_0=\dim W_H^+-\dim W_{H_0}^+$. Equal total dimensions give $-\Phi_0=\dim W_H^--\dim W_{H_0}^-$. The uniform negation is part of the comparison convention; it will also negate integer-valued Hopf classes in degrees divisible by four.

For $q=1$ split $W=W^+\oplus W^-$ by $e_1$. Write the masses as $H=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&g^*\\g&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $H_0=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&g_0^*\\g_0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, where $g,g_0:W^+\to W^-$ are isometries. Clutch on $S^1$ using the two values $I,g_0^{-1}g$ on $S^0$ and subtract the common rank. This defines $\Phi_1$. The original reference identification remains present in $g_0^{-1}g$; replacing it by an abstract isomorphism class of one extended module would discard this datum.

For $q\geq2$, use $e_2$ to identify $W^-$ with $W^+$, making $e_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&I\\I&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The remaining fixed generators and masses have blocks $e_{i+2}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-J_i\\J_i&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $H=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-A\\A&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, with an analogous $A_0$. Direct multiplication gives $J_i^*=-J_i$, $J_i^2=-I$, pairwise anticommutation, $A^*=-A$, $A^2=-I$, and $AJ_i+J_iA=0$, with the same relations for $A_0$. For $x=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{q-2},t)\in S^{q-1}$ define $F(x)=x_0I+\sum_i x_iJ_i+tA$ on $t\geq0$ and $F(x)=x_0I+\sum_i x_iJ_i-tA_0$ on $t\leq0$. The formulas coincide at $t=0$ and satisfy $F^*F=I$ on each hemisphere by the anticommutation identities. They therefore define a based orthogonal clutching map. Let $\Phi_q$ be its reduced clutching class on $S^q$.

Choose positive orthogonal generators $a_1,\ldots,a_8$ on the sixteen-dimensional irreducible $\mathrm{Cl}_{8,0}$ module $S$, and put $\Gamma_8=a_1\cdots a_8$. Then $\Gamma_8^2=I$, $\Gamma_8^*=\Gamma_8$ and $\Gamma_8a_j=-a_j\Gamma_8$. The graded negative $C_8$ module $B$ with grading $\Gamma_8$ and generators $b_j=\Gamma_8a_j$ has ordered volume $b_1\cdots b_8=\Gamma_8$. It is therefore the volume-graded irreducible symbol module of [F4], with $s_8(B)=\beta$. Define $T$ by old fixed generators $E_i=e_i\otimes\Gamma_8$, eight new fixed generators $F_j=1\otimes a_j$, masses $H'=H\otimes\Gamma_8$, $H_0'=H_0\otimes\Gamma_8$, and reference $w'=w\otimes1$. All Clifford and mass identities hold by direct multiplication.

If $A=A_0$, the clutching map factors through the closed upper hemisphere by $t\mapsto|t|$. That disk contracts to the chosen equatorial basepoint while fixing the point, so its clutching map is based nullhomotopic. Common reference blocks contribute zero. Mass homotopies give homotopies of clutching maps; simultaneous coordinate changes conjugate the clutching map and give isomorphic bundles; direct sums give block sums and hence sums of reduced classes. These conclusions hold also in step 1.1 and step 1.2. Reversing the two masses reflects the clutching sphere and negates its class by the reflection/block-rotation proof in [F2]. Thus $\Phi_q$, and consequently $\Psi_q$, respect stable difference relations and inverses.

We compute the actual component generators rather than infer them from the KO table. At $q=0$, real involutions are classified up to orthogonal conjugacy by their eigenspace dimensions; their fixed-rank orbits are real Grassmannians. At $q=1$ the mass parameter is $g\in O(n)$ relative to $g_0$. At $q=2$ it is an orthogonal complex structure $A$, with orbit $O(2n)/U(n)$: an adapted basis consists of pairs $(v,Av)$, and its stabilizer is precisely the complex-linear isometry group. The latter is connected by complex plane rotations, whereas $O(2n)$ has its two determinant components. At $q=4$, the fixed $J_1,J_2$ give a quaternionic multiplicity space. Put $K=J_1J_2$; then $A=KS$ with $S=-KA$ a quaternionic-linear symmetric involution. Its eigenspace orbit is $Sp(k+m)/(Sp(k)\times Sp(m))$. Hence the nonzero stable difference groups in these rows are the real rank difference, the determinant parity, the complex-orientation parity, and the quaternionic rank difference. Their elementary differences are respectively one opposite real line, one reflected real isometry, one reversed complex line, and one opposite quaternionic line.

To identify the exact symbol, first take an OPPOSITE mass pair $(H,-H)$ on a summand. For $q\geq2$, $A_0=-A$, so its transition is the globally linear map $h(x)=x_0I+\sum_i x_iJ_i+tA$. On $W$ put grading $e_1$ and negative-square Clifford generators $c_1=e_1e_2,\ldots,c_{q-1}=e_1e_q,c_q=e_1H$. Each squares to $-I$, is skew-adjoint and odd for this grading, and the generators anticommute. Identify the odd space with the even space by $-e_2$. The even-to-odd blocks then become $I,J_1,\ldots,J_{q-2},A$, respectively. Thus the actual ABS symbol of this graded $C_q$ module $M$ is EXACTLY $h$, and $\Phi_q(H,-H)=s_q(M)$ whereas $\Psi_q(H,-H)=-s_q(M)$. At $q=1$ use grading $e_1$ and generator $e_1H$; the two opposite boundary isometries normalize to $I,-I$ and give the same statement for an elementary reflected line. At $q=0$ the auxiliary positive-rank convention corresponds to the elementary graded real line. This use of a module is confined to an actual opposite DIFFERENCE pair whose reference is retained.

This stabilization is an equivalence of fixed-representation mass problems. The $F_j$ generate $1\otimes M_{16}(\mathbb R)$. An operator anticommuting with every $F_j$, multiplied by $1\otimes\Gamma_8$, commutes with that matrix algebra and hence is $K\otimes1$; consequently the original operator is $K\otimes\Gamma_8$. Matrix units extract its multiplicity space, and multiplication by those units reconstructs it. This recovers the old fixed generators and masses, with their homotopies, sums and reference identifications. The classification of [F1] supplies the same decomposition for every admissible representation of the stabilized fixed algebra. Hence $T:D_q\to D_{q+8}$ is an isomorphism. In particular it transports the elementary component generators from step 2.2 and common folded-null blocks from step 2.1 to all nonnegative degrees.

For completeness, the other four multiplicity models have connected mass spaces. At $q=3$, a further complex structure anticommuting the fixed one is a quaternionic structure on a complex space, with orbit $U(2n)/Sp(n)$. At $q=5$, the two quaternionic isotypic halves must have equal dimension and a mass is an isometry between them, giving $Sp(n)$. At $q=6$, an orthogonal quaternionic-linear complex structure has orbit $Sp(n)/U(n)$: its complex $+i$ eigenspace and its right-$j$ image provide an adapted quaternionic frame. At $q=7$, a further anticommuting structure determines an antiunitary involution on that eigenspace, hence a real form, with orbit $U(n)/O(n)$. These descriptions follow by diagonalizing the fixed Clifford algebra of [F1] and taking adapted frames; their stabilizers are exactly the transformations commuting with the indicated structures. Each quotient is connected because $U$ and $Sp$ are connected, the latter by quaternionic-frame induction over the connected sphere fibrations. Thus $D_3,D_5,D_6,D_7$ vanish. The parity and equal-rank conditions are imposed on admissible representations before stabilization.

A reflected real line in step 1.2 gives transition values $+1,-1$ on $S^0$, so transport around the clutched line returns a vector to its negative. This is the Möbius line and is nonzero stably because its determinant is negative. At $q=2$ take $A=J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $A_0=-J$ on one complex line. The two hemispheres in step 1.3 combine to $F(x_0,t)=x_0I+tJ$, the one-turn rotation on $S^1$ and the underlying real transition of the complex Hopf line. Its lift to $S^3\to SO(3)$ is $\cos(\theta/2)+k\sin(\theta/2)$, which runs from $1$ to $-1$, so it is not nullhomotopic. The stable inclusion preserves its nonzero class by [F3]. Replacing the direction of the difference negates this class, which does not change a group of order two. Thus $\Psi_1$ and $\Psi_2$ send the actual parity generators to the stated actual bundle generators.

For $q\geq1$, apply step 2.3 to the stabilized opposite pair, using grading $E_1=e_1\otimes\Gamma_8$. Its negative generators, in order, are the old $c_1\otimes1,\ldots,c_{q-1}\otimes1$, then $e_1\otimes b_1,\ldots,e_1\otimes b_8$, then $c_q\otimes1$. Move the last coordinate across the eight new coordinates. This is an even permutation, so its orthogonal action is homotopic to identity and introduces no suspension sign. The resulting ordered module has generators $c_i\otimes1$ and $\Gamma_M\otimes b_j$, and grading $\Gamma_M\otimes\Gamma_8$, where $\Gamma_M=e_1$. It is literally $M\widehat\otimes B$. The actual symbol product in [F4] gives $\Phi_{q+8}(T\delta)=s_{q+8}(M\widehat\otimes B)=\Phi_q(\delta)\boxtimes\beta$ for every elementary opposite pair. Uniform negation gives the same identity for $\Psi$, since $-(u\boxtimes\beta)=(-u)\boxtimes\beta$.

Check the integer base case and its sign separately. Stabilizing the POSITIVE-rank elementary difference $(+1,-1)$ produces opposite masses $\Gamma_8,-\Gamma_8$ on $S$. Its module from step 2.3 has grading $a_1$ and negative generators $a_1a_2,\ldots,a_1a_8,a_1\Gamma_8$. Their ordered product is $a_1$: multiplying eight pairs contributes $(-1)^{28}=1$, and $(a_2\cdots a_8)^2=-1$ cancels the sign from moving $a_1$ past seven factors. Thus it is the volume-graded irreducible $C_8$ module. Classification identifies it with $B$, and the grading intertwines because it is the same volume element; polar normalization makes an algebraic intertwiner orthogonal without changing its Clifford action. Consequently its RAW $\Phi_8$ class is $+\beta$. Reversing the difference to the NEGATIVE-rank generator $(-1,+1)$ gives raw $\Phi_8=-\beta$, hence final $\Psi_8=+\beta$. Since $\Psi_0(-1,+1)=+1$, this proves $\Psi_8(T\delta)=\Psi_0(\delta)\boxtimes\beta$ with the stated native negative-rank convention. There is no volume-sign obstruction and no silent reversal of $\beta$.

At $q=4$ use $J_1=L_i,J_2=L_j,K=L_k$ on one quaternionic line. For $S=+1,S_0=-1$, the transition is $F(x_0,x_1,x_2,t)=L_{x_0+x_1i+x_2j+tk}$, exactly the quaternionic Hopf transition. Thus $\Phi_4$ gives the positive Hopf class for a POSITIVE-rank difference. The negative-rank generator is instead $S=-1,S_0=+1$: its $\Phi_4$ value is the negative Hopf class, and its $\Psi_4=-\Phi_4$ value is the positive Hopf class. The source-minus-target/volume convention of [F4] identifies the latter with the chosen generator. Arbitrary involutions are connected to diagonal ones with the same real or quaternionic ranks; common sign blocks give the folded-null transition in step 2.1. Therefore these elementary computations prove $\Psi_q$ is an isomorphism in rows $0,1,2,4$. Steps 3.2 and [F5] prove it for the four zero rows.

In each of the first eight rows, every stable component difference is a sum of the elementary opposite differences and common null blocks identified in step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.2 and step 4.1. Step 3.1 transports this generating description through every eighth row. Additivity, homotopy invariance and step 3.4 and step 3.5 therefore prove $\Psi_{q+8}T=(-\Phi_{q+8})T=\beta\boxtimes(-\Phi_q)=\beta\boxtimes\Psi_q$ on every class. Since $T$ and product by $\beta$ are isomorphisms, induction from the low rows in step 4.1 proves that every $\Psi_q$ is an isomorphism. All constructions retained the fixed reference identification $w$; abstract isomorphism of the modules attached to two separate masses was never used as a substitute for the difference. This proves the stated finite-model comparison with the exact negative-eigenspace and volume conventions.
